tosafot:a1.1: In brief: The one who teaches “they are sacrificed” is Rabbi Shimon, who says one may bring sacrificial animals to a situation of disqualification. [1] Although a peace offering requires leaning [semikha] and the tithe does not (Menaḥot 92a), we are not concerned, since leaning is not indispensable. Tosafot gather many sources that seem to sacrifice an animal without its leaning: the uncircumcised and the impure send their offerings (Pesaḥim 62a); the two nazirites who bring on condition (Nazir 57a); the animal found between Jerusalem and Migdal Eder (Shekalim 7:4); the heir who brings his father’s offering; the leper’s guilt offering and log of oil (Zevaḥim, HaTa’arovet); the mourner and the excommunicated in Mo’ed Katan 15b, and Israel in the wilderness who sent their offerings; “a bull and a calf” (Menaḥot 107a); and the priest who waves for one who sends his offering from overseas (Menaḥot 62b). [2] Against them stand Gittin 28b (“but it requires leaning!”, answered: a bird or a women’s offering), Pesaḥim 89a (the leftover Pesaḥ is not brought on condition because of leaning) and Zevaḥim 74b (offerings intermingled with offerings). [3] Answer: an offering with no remedy by grazing, which would otherwise go to its death, is sacrificed without leaning; one that can be remedied by grazing is not. So the Shekalim case and the heir go without leaning, while intermingled offerings, which can graze, do not. The other sources are set aside one by one: the leper’s guilt offering, since rectifying a man is different; the mourner and the excommunicated with a bird or a women’s offering; the wilderness with the daily offering; the bull and calf with communal burnt offerings; the uncircumcised and impure, who are not fit for leaning and cannot wait; and the waving priest with them or with an heir, per Rabbi Yehuda that an heir does not lean. Our passage, the shared sin offering and the nazirites differ, since from the time they were designated they could not have leaning done. Alternatively, here each animal at its sacrifice may not require leaning at all. [4] And if you ask how they can be offered here at all, when the blood placements of tithe and peace offering differ, one being four placements and the other one: this is a dispute in Zevaḥim 80a over four-placement blood mixed with one-placement blood. Rabbi Eliezer says it is placed as four; Rabbi Yehoshua says as one, since any blood of four placements that was placed as one has fulfilled the obligation; and Rabbi Eliezer holds that the excess is offered up as mere wood. That passage, however, implies that Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Eliezer, regarding “the next day he brings his guilt offering,” that one offers it up as wood. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a2.1: It is a substitute: and the substitute of a tithe is not sacrificed but dies.
gershom:a1.1: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that the substitute of a tithe dies: like the substitute of a sin offering.
rashi:a4.1: According to what he holds: for this is what he says: according to me, since I hold that the substitute of a tithe is not sacrificed, [the eleventh] is not a substitute, for if it were a substitute it would not be sacrificed.
gershom:a2.1: And if you say Rabbi Meir [is speaking] according to what he holds: he says it for himself, for according to Rabbi Meir it is sacrificed, and according to Rabbi Yehuda it dies.
rashi:a4.2: There is no difference between the eleventh, which he called tithe, and ordinary peace offerings, except that this one makes its substitute [fit] to be sacrificed, for peace offerings effect substitution and their substitute is sacrificed; but the eleventh does not make a substitute [fit] to be sacrificed, since Rabbi Yehuda holds that a mistaken tithe is a substitute, and a substitute does not make a substitute. And that last [phrase], “to be sacrificed,” he stated only for the sake of the inference: so it itself is sacrificed as a peace offering.
gershom:a3.1: There is no difference between the eleventh and peace offerings, ordinary ones, except that this one, ordinary peace offerings, makes sanctity to be sacrificed: if one exchanges a non-sacred animal for it, its substitute is sacrificed in its place; and the eleventh’s substitute is not sacrificed.
gershom:a4.1: So it itself is sacrificed: even though he called it a substitute, as he said: “And is there a substitute [that renders a substitute]…”
rashi:a5.1: As it is taught: “If of the herd”: “And if his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings, if he offers of the herd” etc.
gershom:a5.1: “The herd,” to include the eleventh, which is sacrificed as a peace offering: “the herd” is written of peace offerings, as it is written: “And if his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings, if he offers of the herd”; [it is expounded from] the extra letter heh [“the”].
rashi:a6.1: Before it: [the tenth,] which is itself sacred. It stands to reason that it makes a substitute only after it has become sacred.
gershom:a6.1: Even the ninth: as a peace offering.
gershom:a7.1: And does consecration sanctify before it: that is, before it itself is sacred, how can it sanctify what is before it? That is why the ninth is not sanctified, but the eleventh, which is after it, is sanctified.
rashi:a8.1: Interpreted: the [baraita] that teaches “they must die.”
rashi:a8.2: In the present time: he does not hold the view of Rav Huna at the beginning of our chapter (53a), that nowadays animal tithe is not practiced as a decree on account of a purchased animal and an orphan [Rashi’s wording]. Therefore one does not leave them to graze until a blemish befalls them, since in the meantime they might come to a mishap with them, to shearing and work, or come to slaughter them without a blemish. So he puts them into a vaulted chamber [kippa] and they die there of themselves.
tosafot:a8.1: In tithe in the present time: at the beginning of our chapter (53a) we concluded that it is not practiced in the present time because of a mishap; nonetheless, if one did tithe, the name of tithe takes effect on it.
gershom:a8.1: Rather, he interpreted it: the [baraita] that teaches “they must die” is about tithe in the present time, and due to a mishap, so that one should not inflict a blemish on it.
rashi:a9.1: Why specifically two: when two came out as the tenth and he called them “tenth.”
rashi:a10.1: He called the ninth “tenth,” it is sacred: for that does not make him lose it at all, and he eats it with its blemish.
rashi:a10.2: It is not sacred: since it is a peace offering, it makes him lose the breast and the thigh, which go to the priests’ share, and [the owner] can say to him: I did not make you an agent to cause me a loss.
rashi:a10.3: And not to my detriment: and this is the detriment, that he must wait until it is blemished; and further, that it is forbidden to shear it or to work with it.
tosafot:a10.1: He called the ninth “tenth,” it is sacred: Rav Pappi holds that “I sent you to benefit me and not to my detriment” does not apply here, since it is eaten with its blemish, even though one must wait until it becomes blemished and it is forbidden for shearing and work. Alternatively, this is the reason for the eleventh according to Rav Pappi: from the moment the tenth came out, the agent completed his agency, since the tenth is sacred of itself.
gershom:a9.1: He called the ninth “tenth,” it is sacred: for he can eat all of it after a blemish befalls it, without redemption.
gershom:a10.1: [He called] the eleventh “tenth,” it is not sacred: since it makes him lose its breast and thigh; and if he keeps it until a blemish befalls it, it requires redemption, and [the agent] did not carry out his agency.
gershom:a11.1: And not to my detriment: for he cannot eat it unblemished.
gershom:a12.1: In accordance with the intention of the homeowner: according to what he knows of the homeowner’s mind, whether he is generous or not. For they said: a generous eye, one in forty; an average one, one in fifty; a mean eye, one in sixty; as it is written: “So you too shall set apart” [Numbers 18:28], according to your own mind.
rashi:a12.1: He subtracted ten: he separated one in forty, with a generous eye.
rashi:a13.1: That is why I estimated you: for I estimated in my mind that this was your wish, to separate as much as I separated.
rashi:a13.2: You should not have made a mistake: therefore that mistake counts for nothing.
gershom:a13.1: [If he subtracted ten or added] ten, his teruma is teruma: because there are those who separate this way and those who separate that way, he can say: that is how I estimated you, that this is your mind to separate, as some separate so; therefore his teruma is teruma. But here, with the tithe, the homeowner can say to him: you should not have made a mistake; rather, you should have called the one that was certainly the tenth “tenth.”
gershom:a14.1: We will return to you, Ma’aser Behema.
gershom:a15.1: [After the end of the chapter, Rabbeinu Gershom adds a list of six rulings in which the halakha follows Beit Shammai.] In these six halakhot [the halakha is] like Beit Shammai. [The first:] Beit Shammai say one washes the hands and afterward sweeps the house, and Beit Hillel say etc. And the halakha follows Beit Shammai, as Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Ḥananya said that Rav Huna said: In the entire mishna the halakha follows Beit Hillel, except for this, where it follows Beit Shammai [Berakhot 52b].
gershom:a16.1: The second: one who ate and forgot and did not recite the blessing [after the meal]: Beit Shammai say he must return to his place and bless, and Beit Hillel say he blesses in the place where he remembered. And the halakha follows Beit Shammai, since we hold that there are things that require their blessing afterward in their place; and what are they? Bread.
gershom:a17.1: The third: a sukka that does not have four cubits but holds his head, most of his body and his table. Rav Huna said (Sukka 3a): The halakha is that it must hold his head, most of his body and his table. Rabbi Abba said to him: In accordance with whom? Beit Shammai? He said to him: Rather, in accordance with whom? And some say [he answered]: Who is it? Beit Shammai; do not move from it. And after the difficulties we say that they disagree in two things, a large sukka and a small sukka; the halakha follows Beit Shammai about the small sukka, as Rav Shmuel said that Rav Kahana said, and the halakha does not follow Beit Shammai about the large sukka.
gershom:a18.1: And two in the tekhelet [the ritual fringes]: How many threads does one put in? Beit Shammai say four and Beit Hillel say three. How far must they hang down? Beit Shammai say four fingerbreadths and Beit Hillel say three. And the halakha follows Beit Shammai in both, as Rav Pappa said: The halakha is four [threads], within three [fingerbreadths of the edge], hanging four [fingerbreadths].
gershom:a19.1: The sixth: a linen sheet with ritual fringes: Beit Shammai exempt it and Beit Hillel obligate it. Even though we say the halakha follows Beit Hillel, Rava said: it is a decree on account of a night garment; [so here] the halakha follows Beit Shammai, and so is the halakha.
